title: Matching of signal, noise and hardware timescales for filtering and forecasting of correlated noise signals
authors: Joshua Donald, Alex Gabbitas, Arthur G. T. Coveney, Sergey Savel'ev, Pavel Borisov
abstract: Physical reservoir computing exploits the nonlinear dynamics of physical systems to process time-dependent data with greater energy efficiency than conventional machine learning approaches. However, physical reservoirs have fixed intrinsic response timescales, whereas real-world signals combine deterministic and stochastic components across multiple timescales. Here we show, using a nanoporous niobium oxide reservoir, synthetic noisy signals and cryptocurrency-price volatility, that the relationship among noise correlation time, reservoir memory and forecast horizon determines whether correlated noise is filtered or predicted. Noise varying faster than the relevant reservoir memory and forecast horizon is averaged by the reservoir, whereas the temporal structure of slower-varying noise is sufficient for algorithmic forecasting. We introduce the reservoir memory horizon and forecasting regime index to distinguish these operating regimes. These contributions demonstrate that timescale matching can guide the encoding of input time series and development of physical reservoir architectures that filter, analyse and predict stochastic signal components across distinct temporal scales.
summary: This work investigates how physical reservoir computing can be optimized for filtering and predicting complex, noisy signals by precisely matching the timescales of the input noise, the hardware memory, and the required forecast window. Using a niobium oxide device, the authors demonstrate that understanding these timescale relationships allows for the development of new physical architectures capable of analyzing stochastic components across different temporal scales.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of filtering and forecasting correlated noise signals by establishing a relationship between the signal, noise, and hardware timescales.
main_result: Timescale matching is crucial for physical reservoir computing, determining whether the noise is averaged out or if its temporal structure is sufficient for accurate algorithmic forecasting.
method: The authors use a physical reservoir computing setup, testing reconstruction and prediction tasks on synthetic colored noise and real cryptocurrency volatility data.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a nanoporous niobium oxide layer acting as a reservoir. The input signal is modeled as a sum of deterministic harmonics and colored noise, $\xi(t)$.
key_observables: Normalized Root Mean Square Error (NRMSE), Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), Reservoir Memory Horizon, and Forecasting Regime Index.
important_parameters: Noise correlation time ($	au$), reservoir memory, and forecast horizon are the key interacting timescales.
main_assumptions: The performance of the physical reservoir is hypothesized to be governed by the matching of the three relevant timescales.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the reservoir signal processing overview, SNR vs. noise level, and performance metrics (NRMSE) for reconstruction and prediction across varying noise correlation times.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the problem (timescale matching) to detailing the physical setup and signal model, presenting results on reconstruction and prediction using synthetic and real-world data, and concluding with design principles based on operating regimes.
why_interesting: While focused on signal processing, the use of a physical, non-linear, time-dependent system (the reservoir) to process complex, multi-timescale data echoes concepts in open quantum systems where environmental coupling dictates observable dynamics.
